Md Khurshid Alam Khan, Advocate — For the Petitioner.

M Saleem Ullah ------ Petitioner
vs
Dhaka City Corporation represented by Mayor and others ------ Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
2. The facts of the case, in brief, is that the petitioner as plaintiff filed the suit for Specific Performance of Contract being Title Suit No. 5 of 1994 before the Court of Assistant Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka stating, inter alia, that Maghbazar Kutcha Bazar near Maghbazar railway crossing under Police Station, Ramna, Dhaka originally belonged to Dr. Subhan Abdul Kader, Md Sultan and others who subsequently, allowed Maghbazar Bebashahi Samity (Merchants Association) to run a Kutcha Bazar (Kitchen Market) on their land and the Samity, in turn, allowed different persons to run business by constructing their own shop-rooms thereon at their own cost and on condition to pay ground rents/tolls daily. That the plaintiff also took a piece of land and made thereon a shop-room at Maghbazar Kutcha Market PS Ramna, Dhaka on payment of ground rent and it was numbered as shop-room No. 2. The entire bazar was known as holding No. 597 and subsequently, Md Sultan Miah, son of Abdul Kader, Member used to collect the rents on daily basis without any receipt from the plaintiff-petitioner. The owners of the land were entitled to daily rents (tolls) for the use and occupation of their land. The said Kutcha Bazar was subsequently, taken over by the Dhaka Municipal Corporation under the law relating to Hat and Bazar and the corporation realised daily tolls from the plaintiff-petitioner till 20-10-1983 when the defendant-opposite party No. 4 by his memo No. Bazar/2081(1-216) dated 20-10-1983 directed the plaintiff-petitioner to pay the ground rent on monthly basis at the rate of Taka 40/- per month instead of daily tolls/rent. Subsequently opposite party No. 4 by his Memo No. 3016 (1-216) dated 24-10-1983 informed the plaintiff-petitioner that the defendants had decided to construct a pucca market on the land of Kutcha Market and requested the plaintiff-petitioner to shift his business temporarily with a condition that after the construction of pucca market the plaintiff-petitioner would get one shop room in the newly constructed pucca market under the terms and conditions that may be subsequently communicated. The defendant opposite party No. 4 subsequently, by Memo No. Bazar/6728(1-216) dated 12-3-1984 directed the plaintiff-petitioner to pay the first instalment of salami of Taka 10,000/- in two equal installments and to submit 3 recent passport-size photographs of the plaintiff-petitioner. Thereafter, the defendant-opposite party No. 4 by the Memo No. Bazar/7078(1-215) dated 15-4-1984 informed that the Corporation was pleased to allow the payment of salami of first instalments in 5 equal installment of Taka 2,000/- each. The plaintiff at once accepted the said proposal and agreed to pay the salami as demanded by the defendants and in compliance with the aforesaid Memo dated 15-4-1984 the plaintiff deposited Taka 2,000/- by Dhaka Municipal Corporation chalan and submitted 3(three) passport size photographs to the Corporation on 17-4-1984. The plaintiff-petitioner by the subsequent challans dated 7-5-1984, 7-6-1984, 16-7-1984 and 18-8-1984 paid in total Taka 8,000/- to the defendants as full payment of Taka 10,000/- of first instalments of salami for one shop room in Boro Maghbazar Municipality Pucca Market. The plaintiff-petitioner performed his part of the aforesaid contract. The defendant-opposite party Corporation realised the ground rent from the plaintiff-petitioner till March 1986 pending allotment of the shop room in the proposed market. Subsequently, the defendant opposite party stopped taking ground rents and on inquiry from the office of the defendant opposite-parties the plaintiff-petitioner came to know that as he was not using or occupying the land/market of the Corporation they have stopped taking rents. Subsequently, the defendant opposite party constructed one-storied pucca market at Maghbazar Katcha Market and allotted the shops constructed in the ground floor of the said market to different shopkeepers but some of the shops were not allotted /given to anyone. The plaintiff-petitioner was in the hope that he would be given one of those vacant shop-rooms. Subsequently, it transpired that some interested persons in collusion with the officials of the defendant opposite party with malafide intention to deprive the real owners of the shops of the former kutcha market including the plaintiff-petitioner invited tenders to sell the vacant shop at much higher salami for their personal gain and benefit. Thereafter, the plaintiff petitioner by his learned Advocate Ms Lutfunnahar Lucky served a notice dated 20-3-1990 upon the opposite party Nos. 1 & 4 calling upon them to perform their part of the contract. The defendants-opposite parties received the notice but did not make any reply. Thereafter the plaintiff waited for considerable time and after the fall of the Ershad Government and restoration of democratic Government the plaintiff-petitioner through his learned Advocate served another notice dated 21-4-1992 by way of reminder to the defendants-opposite parties calling upon them to perform their part of the contract. The defendant-opposite parties received the notice dated 21-4-1992 but made no reply. Thereafter the petitioner amended his plaint in which he stated that after completion of the pucca market at the old site of the Maghbazar Kutcha Market the defendant-opposite parties did not perform their part of contract by handing over the shop premises to the plaintiff-petitioner and in breach did not hand over the shop premises to the plaintiff and they are in wrongful possession of the shop premises. They are realising rents or profits in wrongful possession of such shop premises and they are liable to pay compensation for the breach of contract and, as such, the defendants opposite parties are liable to pay compensation, naturally being the value of the mesne profits, which the plaintiff-petitioner could have obtained between the date when breach of contract took place and the date when the possession will actually be restored to the plaintiff-petitioner. The defendants-opposite parties are liable to pay mesne profits for the suit property to the plaintiff-petitioner 3(three) years prior to the institution of the suit land till the date of delivery of possession past, pendente lite and future with 20% interest per quarter thereon till realisation of the compensation/mesne profits, from the defendants opposite Parties jointly and severally. The plaintiff-petitioner provisionally assess the compensation (mesne profits) at Taka 1000/- (one thousand) only and the plaintiff-petitioner undertakes to pay additional Court fees on the mesne profits finally assessed by the Court in accordance with law. Accordingly, the prayer portion of the plaint has been amended. The opposite parties as defendants contested the said suit by filing a written statements denying the material allegations made in the plaint alleging, inter alia, that the plaintiff has got no legal character, right, title or any cause of action to file the suit against any of the defendants-opposite Parties. The opposite parties further stated that the plaintiff's suit and claim being illegal, false, malafide, non-maintainable, speculative, vexatious he is not entitled to get the suit decreed. The mandatory notices under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure and section 163 of the Dhaka City Corporation Ordinance, 1983 not having been served on the defendant corporation the plaintiff is not entitled to file the suit or to get any decree as prayed for. The plaintiff's suit and claim is to all intents and purpose a suit for consequential relief and, as such, the suit has been illegally valued and insufficiently stamped. The suit is barred by the provisions of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The opposite parties Corporation is a body corporate, one of the biggest business organisations in charge of various essential and emergency development works, for the better interest of the people being guided and controlled by its own rules and regulations, laws and bye-laws made under its Ordinance. The kutcha bazar situated at Bara Maghbazar, originally belonged to Government, and the ADC (Rev.) duly transferred it to Dhaka City Corporation for running by dismantling and constructing the same with necessary precautions for the better interest of the people. As per rules and regulations, laws and bye-laws made under its Ordinance the opposite parties Corporation are bound to do the needful and are going to do the same for the better interest of the real owners without having any malafide intention to deprive any of them. The act and conduct of the undaunted and litigious plaintiff as third party, who has no right, title, interest and possession as prayed for any shop room at Maghbazar Municipal Corporation Market who has neither any business transaction with the defendant Corporation nor come to Court with clean hands which is outcome of personal grudge and malafide suppression of real facts. Thereafter, the, opposite parties prayed for amendment of the said written statement in which they stated that before demolishing of the Market, 218 shopkeepers were trading in the old market and the Corporation had decided to construct a modern two-storied shopping complex in place of the old market and committed to accommodate them in the proposed market. As per plan ground floor was completed and 161 shopkeepers have been accommodated as per list of the shop-keepers of the old market. But due to insufficient fund the defendant Corporation could not proceed with the construction of the second floor of the market and for that reason 57 shopkeepers of the old market could not be accommodated in the new constructed market but they would be accommodated as per commitment after the completion of the second floor of the market. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka after hearing both parties by the impugned judgment and decree dated 29-6-2002 (decree signed on 6-7-2002) in Title Suit 178 of 2001 decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff-petitioner. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid impugned judgment and decree dated 26-6-2002 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 178 of 2001 the opposite parties as appellants preferred an appeal being Title Appeal NO. 521 of 2002 before the Court of District Judge, Dhaka on 14-10-2002. The said appeal is out of time by 57 days. Hence the opposite parties prayed for condonation of the said delay in filing the appeal. It is stated in the aforesaid application for condonation of delay that the opposite parties stated that the opposite party No. 1 being a corporate body needed decision and approval from its many high officials to sue or appeal before the Honourable Court and, as such, after obtaining certified copy from the learned lawyer 57 days has been delayed to file the appeal as because some of the high officials were not available in their office at the relevant period and accordingly, they prayed for condonation of delay for the ends of justice. It is stated that the present petitioner as respondent contested the said application under section 5 of the Limitation Act by filing written objection stating that it is a matter of record that opposite parties have taken money after allotment of a shop room out of 152 rooms constructed at the old site of Maghbazar Kutcha Bazar near Moghbazar Railway Crossing under the Police Station Ramna, Dhaka. But subsequently, a section of officials through underhand dealing increased the number of allotments of shops and inflated the number from 152 to 215 and for illegal gain allotted the shops to ghost shopkeepers/shop owners. The plaintiff-petitioner was deprived of his legitimate right to get a shop room in place of his old shop room. For more than 20 years the opposite parties officials have been depriving the plaintiff-petitioner, which ultimately compelled him to file the suit for specific performance of contract. The defendants officials concealed many facts but ultimately accepted that there are as many as 50 shops still lying vacant. Under these facts and circumstances, the suit was decreed on contest but the officials of the City Corporation have not yet finished with their cunning and inhuman attitude towards the plaintiff and, as a result, they compelled the filing of the above noted appeal that has already become time barred and a valuable right has accrued to the plaintiff-petitioner and, as such, the application for condonation of delay is liable to be rejected with costs. The defendants have not explained each day of their delay and who are the person or persons responsible for the delay in filing the appeal and that what action the Corporation has taken against its officials who are allegedly liable for the delay and, as such, the application for condonation of delay in filing the above noted appeal is liable to be rejected. In fact, the appeal is a counter-blast of the appeal filed by the respondent for realisation of compensation within the meaning of section 19 of the Specific Relief Act. That the statement made in paragraph No. 3 of the application for condonation of delay so far as it relates to the allegations that the appellant No. 1 being a Corporate body needed decision and approval. from its many high officials to sue or file appeal before the Hon'ble Court and, as such, after obtaining certified copy from the learned lawyer of the appellants 57 days has been delayed to file the appeal as because some of the high officials were not available in the office at the relevant period and, as such, 57 days unwilling delay would graciously be pleased to condone for ends of justice, otherwise the opposite parties will be highly prejudiced are not correct, hence denied that the defendants are to supply strict proof of the same. It is also stated that the defendant& are playing hide and seek game with the learned Court. The defendants have not come before the Hon'ble court with clean hands to get the equitable relief against the rights accrued to the plaintiff-petitioner with the elapse of time and, as such, the power to condone the delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act should be sparingly used and/or it should not be used in a mechanical way, but it must, be used judiciously and in a fit case not in, a case where the whole purpose is tainted with malafide and for collateral purpose and, as such, the application for condonation of, delay is liable to be rejected with cost. The learned District Judge, Dhaka by the order dated 9-1-2003 admitted the appeal and condoned the delay of 57 days without assigning any cogent reason in a slip-shod manner. Being aggrieved by the impugned order dated 9-1-2003 passed by the learned District Judge in admitting the appeal after condonation of delay the plaintiff-petitioner has procured the civil revision before this Court and obtained the instant Rule. 

 4.  Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner, submits that the learned District Judge committed an error of law in passing the impugned order admitting the appeal after condonation of delay of 44 days without assigning any cogent reasons in slipshod manner which has resulted in an error in decision occasioning failure of justice. He then contends that in passing any judicial order a Court of law should assign reason in passing of his decision which is essential to enable the superior Courts and also the litigant public to see as to how a subordinate Court has exercised its judicial mind in passing the order in question. But in the instant case the learned District Judge should not have exercised his judicial discretion by mute or non-speaking orders in slipshod manner which is an error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr Alam contends that negligence of an appellant's officer or his agent or his pleader's clerk is not a sufficient cause within the meaning of section 5 of the Limitation Act for the admission of an appeal filed beyond limitation. He contends that the settled principle of law is that, the Court has discretion to condone delay but such and every day of delay has to be explained by the party praying for condonation of delay. In the absence of explanation coming from the side of the party seeking condonation the court of law would not exercise its discretion to condone the delay. In the instant case the opposite parties failed to explain each and every day of delay and, as such, the learned District Judge committed an error of law in condoning the delay which is an error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. He finally, submits that the grounds taken for condonation that the opposite party Nos. 2, 3 and 4 are high officials of the corporation, opposite party No. 1 being a corporate body, needed decisions and approval of many officials and also to get a certified copy of the trial. Court judgment and decree and some of the high officials were not available in their office at the relevant period (without mentioning any specific date) there is no good ground for its condonation of delay and, as such, the learned District Judge committed an error of law in condoning the delay of 44 days which is an error in the impugned judgment and order occasioning failure of justice. He finally, submits that the learned District Judge considering this ground of condonation committed an error of law in admitting the appeal, which has resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 6. I have perused the impugned judgment and order, the application for condonation of delay, supplementary affidavit filed on behalf of the petitioner, counter-affidavit and other materials on record. It appears that in the instant case the suit was decreed in favour of the plaintiff-petitioner on 29-6-2002 by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka (Decree signed on 6-7-2002) in Title Suit No. 178 of 2001. Admittedly, the opposite parties applied for certified copy of the impugned judgment and decree on 18-7-2002 and the same was made ready for delivery on 11-8-2002 and on that date the opposite party obtained the certified copy of the impugned judgment and decree and therefore, the appeal was due to be filed on 29-8-2002 but due to the necessity for obtaining opinion and approval of lawyer and higher authorities respectively before filing the appeal there was a delay of 46 days in filing the appeal. In the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act for condonation of delay (Annexure-A) paragraph 3 reads as follows: That the appellant No. 1 is a statutory corporation and the appellant Nos. 2, 3 and 4 are the high officials of that corporation and the appellant No. 1 being a corporate body is to need decisions and approval from its many high officials to sue or appeal before Hon'ble Court and, as such, after obtaining certified copy from the learned lawyer of the Appellant 57 days has been delayed to file this instant appeal as because some of the high officials were not available in their office at the relevant period and, as such, 57 days unwilling delay would graciously be pleased to condone for ends of justice otherwise the appellants will be highly prejudiced.
